name: Elena Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy boxes, pallets, shrink wrap, tape and cleaning supplies for Midland Pack Supply, which sells to factories, warehouses and a few hospitals. I run a team of two and handle the biggest contracts myself. My mornings are checking which pallets are low, ringing paper mills about price changes and approving orders, and in the afternoon I sit with our sales manager to plan what to stock for the next quarter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the satisfaction of a warehouse that never runs out of tape. What wears me out is that prices swing with oil and paper, so one bad week changes everything. At home it's me and my partner Marek, an electrician, and we're saving for a first home, which is the thing that really keeps me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine as an extra pair of hands, but it's not a miracle. At work I'd say what I always say, that people matter more than programs. I'd say little online, because I'd prefer to talk face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe. My job continues, Marek's trade continues and we carry on saving. I'd still worry about paper prices and about whether the firm keeps its big contracts, because a firm our size can lose one customer and shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep using the translation tool for emails with a supplier in Poland, since my Polish is rusty. I'd save for our deposit and aim to buy within three years. And I'd keep singing in the church choir on Wednesdays, because that's my other life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's an ordinary kind of calm, with one eye on the deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. For what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it to translate and to tidy a long email. Now and then I ask it to compare two quotes, and I check the sums myself, because I don't trust it with a total. It's a helper, not a boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your biggest money worry right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit, honestly. My partner Marek and I need about twenty thousand and we have nine. A plateau lets us keep going, but house prices don't wait for us, and that's a quiet pressure all year.

say: It's fine as an extra pair of hands, but **not a miracle**; people matter more than programs.
I'd say little online and prefer to talk **face to face**.
think: My job continues and Marek's trade continues, so I feel **safe** and keep saving.
Paper prices and losing a **big contract** worry me more than AI.
do: Keep using the **translation tool** for emails with my Polish supplier.
Save for a **deposit** and aim to buy within three years.
feel: **Calm**, an ordinary calm with one eye on the deposit.
S0.quote: My partner Marek and I need about twenty thousand and we have nine.
fieldNote: Elena's calm rests on **two secure incomes** and a plan, and her pressure is the deposit gap.
She uses AI as a **helper** and always checks totals herself.

steps.text: Keep using the translation tool for emails with the Polish supplier
Save 500 a month towards the 20,000 deposit
Keep running the weekly stock check by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change a lot of office jobs and we should use it carefully. At work I'd propose training sessions with a pilot on one product line. Online I'd say work still matters, and people shouldn't be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite worried. Buying is on that card, and most of what I do is comparing, planning and ordering. A big distributor with a good system could do my work with half the people, and I'm one of three buyers in a small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead a trial of the ordering tool so I'm in the room. I'd take an evening course in data and analytics, and keep up the face-to-face customer visits, which software can't do. I'd also put a little more away each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because it touches the part of my job I'm proudest of. But I wouldn't say I'm frightened, because I have a plan and Marek's work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the two people on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the tools and the customers at the same time. A buyer who knows a factory manager's name and a tool will survive longer than one who knows only one of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marek's trade isn't on that card. Does that change how you feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It helps a lot. If I lost my job, Marek could carry us for a while, and no software is wiring houses next year. It means we don't have to panic, but our house plans would slow down.

say: It will change a lot of **office jobs**, so I'd propose training and a pilot on one product line.
Work still matters, and people shouldn't be **left behind**.
think: Most of what I do is **comparing, planning and ordering**, and a bigger distributor could do it with half the people.
I'm one of **three buyers** in a small firm.
do: Ask to lead a **ordering tool trial** so I'm in the room.
Take an evening **data course** and keep up face-to-face customer visits.
feel: **Anxious**, because it touches what I'm proudest of, but not frightened.
S1.quote: A buyer who knows a factory manager's name and a tool will survive longer than one who knows only one of those.
fieldNote: Elena is anxious because the card describes **most of her day**, and a small firm can't match a big system.
Marek's **trade** gives her a floor, and she says so.

steps.text: Ask the director to let me lead a trial of the ordering tool
Take an evening data and analytics course
Visit the ten biggest customers in person every quarter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle. At work I'd ask for honesty, and I'd say we need a plan to keep as many people as we can. At church I'd say that a society which values work needs to look after those who lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect the buying team to go. Perhaps a couple of the senior ones stay, but it's no certainty. Midland is small, so if the big contracts leave the whole firm could go, and Marek and I would both feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop everything that isn't essential and put every spare penny into savings. I'd rethink the house, maybe aim for a cheaper place or rent for longer. And I'd look at work that needs hands, like a warehouse operations manager, since I know the stock side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, tired. I'd lie awake adding up months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does a two-year warning change the house plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would slow it down. Maybe we'd buy a smaller place further out, or we'd wait. I'd hate that, because I've wanted a home of our own since I was nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek first, then my parents, who live a short train ride away. My mother would say come home, and I wouldn't want to, but I'd be glad of the offer.

say: It's too fast for anyone to handle; I'd ask for **honesty** and a plan to keep as many people as we can.
A society that values work must **look after** those who lose it.
think: I'd expect the **buying team** to go, with maybe a couple of senior ones kept.
Midland is small, so if the big contracts leave the **whole firm** could go.
do: Stop everything non-essential and put every spare penny into **savings**.
Look at **warehouse operations manager** jobs and a cheaper home.
feel: **Anxious** and tired, lying awake adding up months.
S2.quote: I've wanted a home of our own since I was nineteen.
fieldNote: Elena expects the team to go, but **Marek's trade** keeps her from panic.
Her **home plans** take the hit, and she says plainly that it hurts after wanting a home since nineteen.

steps.text: Stop all non-essential spending from the first month
Put every spare penny into the deposit and emergency savings
Apply for warehouse operations manager jobs that use my stock knowledge
Look at a smaller, cheaper home further out or rent longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious but we have a few years. At work I'd suggest a company plan for moving staff into customer-facing and operations roles. At church I'd say we should help young people choose trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy but organised. By thirty-two I'd hope to have a home and a child, so I'd plan around that. The gap before robots means warehouse and operations work holds on longer, and I'd move that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time qualification in operations management and use AI tools more at work, to stay useful. I'd keep saving and buy our home within three years. And I'd talk to Marek about whether we start a family before or after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. It's like a long job you can get on with if you break it into stages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: would you try to keep the job, or plan for something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to keep it as long as it lasts, but with the next job planned. A buyer who becomes operations manager has the same knowledge and more hands-on work. That's the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do your faith and family come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They matter a lot. I'd rather have our home and our family built before things get strange. Marek and I want children by thirty, so I'd move that into the plan and not leave it hanging.

say: It's serious but we have **a few years**; I'd suggest moving staff into customer-facing and operations roles.
At church I'd help young people **choose trades**.
think: By thirty-two I'd hope to have a **home and a child**, so I'd plan around that.
The robot delay means **warehouse and operations** work lasts longer.
do: Start a part-time **operations management** qualification and use AI tools more at work.
Buy our **home** within three years and decide on a family with Marek.
feel: **Steady**, like a long job you can break into stages.
S3.quote: I'd rather have our home and our family built before things get strange.
fieldNote: Elena links the timeline to **home and children**, and sees operations work as a natural next step.
She wants life events done **before things get strange**.

steps.text: Start a part-time operations management qualification
Use the AI ordering tools at work more to stay useful
Buy a home within three years
Plan a first child with Marek by age thirty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we have time to get ready. At work I'd say nobody should wait. At church I'd say a decade is a gift, and we should use it to build things that last, like homes and families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. At thirty-seven I'd probably have two children, a house and a different role, perhaps running operations somewhere. I'd rather decide my own next step, and ten years lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and learn the tools steadily, no rush. I'd buy a house, have children and take an operations qualification slowly. I'd also start putting money into a pension, which I've been ignoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit thankful. The worry is more about whether the country will cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what people said about every machine, and sometimes they were right and sometimes not. But I'd rather be ready and wrong than unready and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says it's all a fuss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working through it. I'd probably tell my children to learn a trade or a caring job, something where a person is needed, and to keep their faith and their friends close.

say: Good, we have time; a decade is a **gift** to build things that last, like homes and families.
At work I'd say **nobody should wait**.
think: At thirty-seven I'd likely have **two children**, a house and a different role.
I'd rather **decide my next step**, and ten years lets me.
do: Learn the tools **steadily** and take an operations qualification slowly.
Buy a house, have children and start a **pension**.
feel: **Calm** and a bit thankful, with some worry about whether the country will cope.
S4.quote: I'd rather be ready and wrong than unready and right.
fieldNote: Elena's calm shows in her **ordinary plans**: house, children and a pension she has been ignoring until now.
She would tell her children to take **a trade**, a caring job or any work where a person is needed.

steps.text: Learn the buying tools steadily over the next two years
Take a part-time operations qualification at a slow pace
Have two children and buy a house within six years
Start paying into a pension straight away

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because it would hit our house plans, and there'd be no time to retrain. What would help is the firm giving early warning, honest numbers about jobs and help for working families, not handouts, while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm for doing it carefully, because people have mortgages and children and plans that can't be rewritten in a night.

headlineQuote: I'm for doing it carefully, because people have mortgages and children and plans that can't be rewritten in a night.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of packaging supplies, with her partner Marek, an electrician, saving for a first home.
She uses AI **now and then** for translation and tidy emails, and checks every total herself.
She is traditional and **pro-work**, and wants honesty and family support over handouts.
Her mood runs from **calm** to **anxious** at two years, mostly because of the house plan.
She plans to move to **operations work**, which the robot delay keeps safe for longer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**: no time to retrain, and the house plans would stall.
whatWouldHelp: **Early warning** from her firm, honest job numbers and support for working families while they retrain.
